segments.text: The first stealth aircraft the world saw was shaped like a diamond, with flat panels and
sharp angles that look like something drawn with a ruler.
It was not designed that way because the engineers thought it was elegant.
It was designed that way because the computers of the 1970s were only able to calculate
how radar bounces off flat surfaces.
Curves were beyond them.
The shape that changed air warfare was, in part, the shape the arithmetic of the time
could handle.
So here is the question.
How do you make a 10-ton metal machine nearly vanish from a radar, and why has it never
quite vanished?
The answer begins with a correction.
A stealth aircraft is not invisible.
It is built to return less, to return it in the wrong direction, and to be heard from
a shorter distance.
Each part of the design exists because the part before it reduces the echo and leaves
some of it behind.
Start with the radar's own problem from the earlier video in this series.
A radar needs a little of its signal to come back to the antenna.
A stealth aircraft's main trick is to make sure that very little does.
Instead of letting the beam bounce straight back, the surface is tilted so that the beam
is thrown off to one side, like a mirror turned away from a torch.
A plain flat plate at an angle sends the energy upward or downward.
That is the reason for the diamond.
Every facet is tilted, so that wherever the radar is, most of the energy is deflected into
the sky or the ground.
This explains the odd details in the outline of these aircraft.
The edges of the wings and the tail are lined up at the same few angles, so that when the
radar sweeps across, the strong echoes from the edges all fly off in the same few directions
and not in many.
Doors and panels have saw-toothed edges for the same reason.
Weapons are carried inside the body because a missile hanging under a wing is a brilliant
reflector and an open bay is a hole that gets closed again as quickly as possible.
Even the way the cockpit glass is coated serves the same end.
The other great answer to the same problem was to remove the surfaces altogether.
A flying wing has no tail and no vertical fin, and those are among the strongest reflectors
on a conventional aircraft, because two surfaces at right angles act like the corner of a room
and send the beam straight back.
A flying wing has smooth curves and a saw-toothed back edge, and by now the computers could handle
curves.
It looks organic where the first one looked cut from a sheet.
The idea is the same, but a better calculator allowed a better shape.
Then come the parts that cannot be tilted.
The engines of a jet are a problem, because a radar beam that enters the inlet strikes the
spinning blades and returns a strong echo.
The answer is to hide the engine.
The air intake is curved into an S-shape so that the beam cannot see straight down it, and
the walls are lined with material that absorbs the energy as it bounces.
The exhaust, which is also hot and visible to infrared, is flattened and often sits on
top of the aircraft, so that heat seekers on the ground cannot see it easily.
Absorbing material is the second major tool.
A radar-absorbent coating is made of paint or tiles laced with tiny particles that convert
part of the radio energy into heat as it passes through.
It is not a magic black paint.
It works best over a narrow range of frequencies, adds weight, is easily damaged by rain, sand,
and ordinary handling, and has to be repaired with care.
The earliest stealth aircraft were notorious for this.
A crew spent more hours on the skin than on any other part, and an aircraft with damaged
coating was a different aircraft.
Nobody outside the programs knows how small the echo really is.
The figures are among the most closely guarded in the military, and the numbers that circulate,
a marble, a bird, a golf ball, are guesses or boasts.
What is publicly known is that the echo depends strongly on angle and frequency, so there is no
single number for an aircraft. It has a map of numbers, and the map is a secret.
A defender who does not know the map has to assume a worse case.
There is a price for all these shapes that goes far beyond maintenance.
An aircraft designed to scatter radar is not designed to fly well.
The diamond was aerodynamically unstable, which meant that it could only be flown by a computer
making constant corrections. Carrying weapons internally limits how many can be taken,
so a stealthy strike aircraft carries fewer bombs than an ordinary one.
Fuel has to be carried inside as well. Every choice that reduces the echo takes
something away from the aircraft. The first operational type was awkward in the sky,
and its crews gave it the affectionate nickname of the Wobbling Goblin.
It flew mostly at night, partly because it could not hide from the eye,
and its mission was to slip through gaps in air defenses in the first hours of a war,
and hit the few targets that opened the way for everyone else. It was a very expensive aircraft
with a short list of jobs, which is what a specialist usually is. And there is a deeper
limit, which is wavelength. The shaping tricks work best when the features of the aircraft are much
larger than the radar's wavelength. A long wavelength radar in the very high frequency band
sees the aircraft's overall size and its larger pieces as resonant elements, and the careful tilting
stops helping. These radars are not precise enough to guide a missile, but they can tell that something
is there. This is why stealth is described not as invisibility, but as a reduction in detection
range at the frequencies that matter for shooting. The numbers show how modest and how useful this is.
The echo from a target falls with the fourth power of range, as we saw. So if a stealth design
cuts the echo to a hundredth of what a normal aircraft would give, the range at which a radar can
see it falls to about a third. That is not vanishing. But a third of the range means a third of the
warning, and a missile battery that sees the aircraft only at that distance has a fraction
of the time to react. The design is a way of buying seconds, and seconds are what a defense runs on.
Because the echo varies so much with angle, mission planners treat a stealth sortie as a puzzle
of geometry. They know where the enemy's radars stand and plan a route that keeps the aircraft's
best side toward each one, turning at the right moments so that its strongest echo points at empty
ground. A route is drawn the way a chess player thinks about a diagonal, and a single careless
turn can change a quiet sky into a loud one. It also shows the weakness. A radar that is not looking,
does not see, but one that is looking from the right angle, or from the side, might. A radar that sends
out a signal and listens with receivers at other sites is not looking for echoes that come straight back,
but for those that are sent off sideways, which is just where stealth shaping sends them. Networks of
sensors, rather than single stations, are the answer to a shape that hides from one. In 1999,
a stealth aircraft was shot down over Serbia. Accounts of how, most of them from the Serbian side,
point to a battery that moved often, used older, lower frequency radar, and took advantage of flight
pads that had become predictable. There are other ways to be found as well. An aircraft emits heat,
which infrared sensors can see from a long way. It makes noise, and its engine leaves a trail of
exhaust. It talks on the radio. It uses its own radar and gives itself away. The truly careful
stealth crew treats emissions as a part of the aircraft's shape, keeping the radar off,
flying with sensors passive, and receiving information over a narrow beam. A silent stealth
aircraft, and a noisy one, are different machines, even if the airframe is the same. Which brings us to
what is easy to get wrong. A common idea is that stealth makes an aircraft immune. A more accurate
idea is that it changes who has the initiative. A defender who sees an aircraft late must choose
between shooting blind and waiting. And an attacker who knows this can pick the place and time. That is
my own reading. But it suggests that the key value of stealth is not that it cannot be seen. It is that the
defender no longer gets to decide when they see it. So return to the diamond that came out of a limit in the
arithmetic. Every part of a stealth aircraft, the angled panels, the hidden weapons, the S-shaped inlet,
the coating, and the silence, is there to take a little more time away from the person trying to
find it. Stealth is not the absence of an echo. It is the attempt to make the echo arrive too late to matter.
